title: Opening Port 80 on the Firewall
tagline: Unblock HTTP web traffic in your server firewall settings
briefing: Internet Users are wired to your EC2 server, but when they try to visit your website, the server firewall rejects them because Port 80 is not listed in the allowed rules.
taskDescription:
1. Click the EC2 Web Server on the board.
2. In the right-hand Inspector panel, click "+ Allow Inbound Port 80 (HTTP)".
3. Click "Run Traffic Test".
docTips: Port 80 is standard HTTP web traffic; Port 443 is encrypted HTTPS web traffic.
In AWS, this per-server firewall list is called a "Security Group".

conceptCard.title: What is an AWS Security Group?
conceptCard.summary: In AWS, every EC2 server has a built-in virtual firewall called a Security Group. By default, it blocks all incoming traffic until you explicitly open a port.
conceptCard.analogy: Think of a Security Group like a building receptionist checking visitor badges: unless you tell the receptionist "Allow visitors going to Room 80 (HTTP)", everyone gets turned away at the door.
conceptCard.keyTakeaway: Click the EC2 server and click "+ Allow Inbound Port 80 (HTTP)" in the right-hand panel.

title: Public Zone vs. Private Zone
tagline: Learn why the board is divided into Public and Private network zones
briefing: In AWS, a network is split into zones called Subnets. Public Subnets can receive visitors from the internet, while Private Subnets are hidden in the back. Place an EC2 Web Server inside the Public Subnet and wire Internet Users to it.
taskDescription:
1. Click "+ EC2 Instance" and place it on the glowing target ring in the Public Subnet.
2. Use the "Wire" tool to connect Internet Users to your EC2 server.
3. Click "Run Traffic Test".
docTips: Grid columns in the center (-1 to +2) represent the Public Subnet.
Grid columns on the right (+3 to +7) represent the Private Subnet behind the security barrier.

conceptCard.title: Why Are There Public and Private Zones?
conceptCard.summary: Notice the labeled zones on the 3D board: the middle section is the Public Subnet (teal), and the right-hand section is the Private Subnet (indigo).
conceptCard.analogy: Think of a bank: the Public Subnet is the front lobby where customers walk in from the street (your website). The Private Subnet is the locked back vault where cash and customer records are kept (your database).
conceptCard.keyTakeaway: Web servers that talk directly to Internet Users belong in the Public Subnet.

conceptCard.title: What is an Amazon S3 Bucket?

conceptCard.analogy: If an EC2 server is a chef working at a kitchen counter, an S3 Bucket is a massive, indestructible walk-in pantry where all ingredients and photos are kept safe.

title: Adding a Database in the Private Zone (RDS)
tagline: Store structured user accounts safely behind the Private Subnet barrier
briefing: To save user sign-ups and orders, your EC2 Web Server needs a PostgreSQL database. Place an RDS Database inside the Private Subnet on the right side of the barrier and wire your EC2 server to it.
taskDescription:
1. Click "+ RDS PostgreSQL" and place it on the glowing target ring in the Private Subnet.
2. Wire your EC2 Web Server to the RDS Database.
3. Click "Run Traffic Test".
docTips: PostgreSQL databases communicate over Port 5432 by default.
Keeping RDS in the Private Subnet ensures hackers on the internet cannot directly probe your database.

conceptCard.title: What is Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service)?
conceptCard.summary: While S3 is great for files and photos, structured records (usernames, orders, balances) belong in a SQL database like PostgreSQL running on Port 5432.
conceptCard.analogy: Because databases hold your most sensitive data, you always place them in the Private Subnet on the right side of the barrier—so only your EC2 web server can talk to the database, never outside strangers.
conceptCard.keyTakeaway: Place the RDS Database on the glowing tile in the Private Subnet and wire your EC2 server to it.

conceptCard.title: What is a Load Balancer (ALB)?
conceptCard.summary: If thousands of users visit your site at once, a single EC2 server will slow down or crash. And if that one server reboots, your whole site goes offline.
conceptCard.analogy: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is like an airport dispatcher directing incoming passengers evenly to two open security lanes. If one lane closes, all passengers smoothly go to the other.
conceptCard.keyTakeaway: Place a second EC2 server on the glowing ring and wire the Load Balancer to both EC2 servers.

docTips: You never have to write Terraform code from scratch in CloudCraft—the game generates it live from your 3D blocks so you can learn by seeing.
Clicking the "Terraform Blueprint" button in the bottom dock shows the recipe for your entire board.

conceptCard.title: Demystifying DevOps & "Terraform"
conceptCard.summary: Up until now, you placed servers and clicked settings by hand. In the real world, what if you need to recreate this exact setup 20 times without forgetting a port? That is why DevOps engineers use "Infrastructure as Code" (like Terraform).
conceptCard.analogy: Think of Terraform like architectural blueprints or a LEGO instruction booklet. Instead of remembering which buttons you clicked in AWS, Terraform saves your 3D board as a simple text recipe (`resource "aws_instance" ...`). Whenever you change a block on the board, CloudCraft writes the Terraform recipe for you automatically!
conceptCard.keyTakeaway: We just unlocked the "Terraform Blueprint" button! Click the EC2 server to check its recipe, connect it to the RDS database, and run the test.

stages.title: Stage 1/3 · Initial Deployment & Routing
stages.incidentAlert: INCIDENT BRIEF: Deploy EC2 in their valid AWS zones and wire live traffic from Internet Users.
stages.objectiveSummary: Establish the baseline Amazon EC2 Sizing + t3.micro vs m5.large architecture with zero subnet or firewall violations.
hints: Symptom Clue: Inspect the current board state—traffic from Internet Users cannot complete the journey because key Amazon EC2 Sizing components or wires are missing.
Architecture Concept: Compute (EC2): Keep VPC compute & databases out of the external Edge/DNS zone.
Exact Blueprint: Select "+ EC2" from the dock, place it in the PUBLIC zone, and connect a wire to it.

stages.title: Stage 2/3 · Latency Spike & Cache Acceleration
stages.incidentAlert: LIVE TRAFFIC SURGE: Your Stage 1 deployment is online, but viral traffic just drove p99 Latency to 640ms! Repeated reads are hammering your backend. Slash p99 latency under 85ms!
stages.objectiveSummary: Accelerate read performance by adding an in-memory Redis Cache (in Private Subnet) or CloudFront Edge CDN.
hints: Symptom Clue: Look at the live p99 Latency meter—repeated requests are querying slow backend storage on every single page load.
Architecture Concept: Tech giants like Instagram and Netflix place an in-memory cache (ElastiCache Redis) in the Private Subnet or a CDN (CloudFront) at the Edge to serve hot data in < 2ms.

Exact Blueprint: Select "+ Redis" from the dock, place it inside the PRIVATE SUBNET (right-hand indigo zone), and wire your compute tier (EC2 / Lambda / EKS) to Redis (or wire CloudFront CDN in the Edge zone).

stages.title: Stage 3/3 · Rate-Limit & Security Hardening
